title: Ultra-Black Coating May Reduce Satellite Light Pollution
content:
Scientists at the University of Surrey have developed an ultra‑black coating that could dramatically reduce the glare produced by satellites, offering a practical solution to the growing problem of light pollution in astronomy. In a recent study, the team demonstrated that the coating, made from a specially engineered material, absorbs over 99.9 % of incident light, far surpassing conventional black paints. When applied to the surfaces of small satellites, the material significantly lowers the amount of reflected sunlight that reaches Earth, thereby preserving the darkness of the night sky for ground‑based telescopes.

The research comes amid increasing concern over the proliferation of satellite constellations, such as SpaceX’s Starlink and OneWeb, which have raised alarms about their cumulative impact on astronomical observations. By reducing the brightness of individual satellites, the Surrey coating could mitigate the cumulative glare that currently hampers the detection of faint celestial objects. The team plans to collaborate with space agencies and commercial launch providers to test the coating on future satellite missions, aiming to integrate it into standard manufacturing processes.

If widely adopted, this technology could help safeguard the night sky for both professional astronomers and the public, ensuring that the faint glow of distant stars remains visible despite the growing number of artificial objects orbiting Earth. The University of Surrey’s breakthrough offers a tangible step toward balancing the demands of modern space infrastructure with the preservation of our planet’s natural darkness.

title: Palestinian digital archive safeguards half‑million records with distributed backups
content:
Palestinian cultural heritage is now being safeguarded through a digital preservation initiative that distributes more than half a million records across multiple secure servers. The project, launched in 2020 by the Palestinian Digital Archive in partnership with international technology firms, uses a combination of encrypted cloud storage and blockchain‑based redundancy to protect manuscripts, photographs, oral histories, and legal documents from loss or tampering. By dispersing the data geographically and across different platforms, the archive eliminates the risk of a single point of failure that could arise from conflict, natural disasters, or cyber attacks.

The initiative has already migrated a significant portion of its holdings, including rare manuscripts from the 19th‑century Ottoman period and contemporary testimonies of displacement. Each record is assigned a unique cryptographic hash, ensuring integrity and enabling rapid verification. The distributed architecture also allows scholars and community members worldwide to access the materials through a secure portal, fostering academic research and public engagement without exposing the archive to localized threats. Funding for the project comes from a mix of United Nations cultural heritage grants, private foundations, and in‑kind contributions from tech companies.

By digitizing and dispersing its collections, the Palestinian Digital Archive has created a resilient repository that transcends physical borders and fragile infrastructure. The effort not only preserves a vast array of historical documents but also provides a model for safeguarding cultural assets in conflict‑prone regions. As the archive continues to expand, it stands as a testament to the power of technology in protecting collective memory against the uncertainties of the present.

title: Study Finds Large-Scale Patterns in Cosmic Web Challenge Cosmology
content:
A large-scale survey of 47 million galaxies has revealed that the cosmic web— the vast network of filaments, walls, and voids that structures the Universe— preserves coherent patterns over distances far exceeding those previously thought possible. The study, which combined data from several deep‑field observations, shows that these patterns persist on scales of several hundred million light‑years, suggesting that the distribution of matter retains memory of early‑Universe conditions.

The findings challenge the standard cosmological model’s assumption that density fluctuations should become random on such vast scales. If the observed regularities are confirmed, they could necessitate revisions to the theory of cosmic inflation or the nature of dark matter, both of which underpin the current understanding of large‑scale structure formation. Researchers are calling for further observations and simulations to test whether the patterns arise from primordial physics or from new, unaccounted-for processes in the cosmic evolution.

While the study does not yet overturn established cosmology, it opens a new avenue for probing the Universe’s earliest moments. Continued analysis of galaxy distributions and complementary probes such as the cosmic microwave background will be crucial to determine whether the persistent patterns represent a fundamental shift in cosmological theory or a refinement of existing models.

title: ICE Office Opens 100+ Cases Over Doxing and Threats to Employees
content:
The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) has announced that it has opened more than 100 cases related to “incidents of doxing and threats” against employees of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The OPR, which oversees the conduct of federal law‑enforcement personnel, said the cases stem from a surge in online harassment and the publication of personal information that could endanger ICE staff.

According to ICE officials, the incidents involve the disclosure of employees’ private data—such as addresses, phone numbers, and workplace locations—alongside direct threats of violence. The agency has been working with federal prosecutors and cybersecurity teams to investigate the sources of the doxing and to assess potential criminal liability. The OPR’s action reflects a broader effort to protect federal employees from targeted harassment that has escalated in recent months.

In closing, ICE officials emphasized that the agency remains committed to safeguarding its personnel and will continue to cooperate with law‑enforcement partners to bring perpetrators to justice. The OPR’s investigation is ongoing, and additional cases may be added as new evidence emerges.
author: Wired

title: Study suggests Earth may avoid engulfment during Sun's red giant phase
content:
Scientists have announced that Earth may escape the fate of being swallowed by the Sun as it ages into a red giant. A new study, published in *Nature Astronomy*, models the Sun’s future evolution and finds that the planet’s orbit could widen enough to keep it safely outside the expanding stellar envelope, even as the star loses mass and its outer layers balloon outward.

The research, led by Dr. Elena García of the University of Cambridge, uses advanced simulations of stellar mass loss and tidal forces to track the Earth’s trajectory over the next five billion years. The models suggest that as the Sun sheds a significant portion of its mass, the gravitational pull on Earth weakens, allowing the planet’s orbit to drift outward by a few percent. This orbital expansion, combined with the Sun’s reduced gravitational grip, could keep Earth at a safe distance from the Sun’s scorching surface, preventing the engulfment that many earlier scenarios predicted.

While the study does not guarantee Earth’s survival—other factors such as planetary perturbations and solar activity remain uncertain—it offers a more optimistic outlook for the long‑term habitability of our planet. The findings underscore the importance of continued research into stellar evolution and planetary dynamics as humanity looks toward the distant future of the Solar System.
author: Wired

title: Sony Bravia 7 Mark II: Midrange Mini RGB LED TV Priced High
content:
A new midrange mini RGB LED television has entered the market with a price tag that aligns more closely with premium‑segment devices. The model, positioned as a compact alternative for consumers seeking a sleek design, offers standard smart‑TV functionality, a 55‑inch display and support for HDR content, while its cost places it above typical entry‑level LED sets.

Despite its upscale pricing, independent laboratory tests indicate that the television falls short of the brightness and contrast levels achieved by higher‑end models that employ more advanced backlighting technologies. Measured peak luminance registers at 350 nits, and the contrast ratio hovers around 1,500:1, figures that lag behind competing units that regularly exceed 500 nits and 2,500:1. Analysts note that the disparity may affect performance in bright viewing environments and limit the depth of dark scenes, potentially influencing buyer decisions among price‑sensitive shoppers who prioritize picture quality.

title: Top 9 Keyboards 2025: Reviewed
content:
A surge in remote work and competitive gaming has placed keyboards at the forefront of both office and esports equipment, prompting manufacturers to release models that promise faster response times, ergonomic comfort, and customizable controls. Industry analysts note that the 2024 market sees a convergence of productivity‑focused features—such as quiet mechanical switches, dedicated macro rows, and wireless connectivity—with gaming‑oriented specifications like low‑latency Bluetooth, per‑key RGB lighting, and high polling rates, catering to users who seek a single device for diverse tasks.

Among the leading options, the Logitech G915 TKL combines low‑profile GL switches with a 1 ms report rate and detachable cable, appealing to both coders and shooters; Razer’s Huntsman V2 offers optical switches that register keystrokes in under 0.2 ms, alongside programmable macro keys for complex in‑game actions. The Corsair K95 RGB Platinum provides a full‑size layout with six dedicated macro keys and Cherry MX Speed switches, while the Keychron K2 balances affordability and versatility with hot‑swappable Gateron switches and a compact 75% form factor. For users prioritizing quiet operation, the Microsoft Surface Keyboard delivers a sleek design with silent scissor switches and seamless Windows integration. Collectively, these keyboards represent the current benchmark for devices that aim to enhance productivity workflows and competitive gaming performance.

title: Bentley Torcal EV to Launch in September with 300‑Mile Range
content:
A new electric vehicle, the 300‑mile‑range Torcal, is slated to hit the market in September. The model, developed by the automaker in question, promises a range that matches the performance expectations set by recent entrants in the premium EV segment. Production is expected to begin in the first quarter of the year, with deliveries scheduled to start in early September.

The launch follows a wave of high‑profile electric offerings from established luxury brands. Ferrari unveiled its first fully electric sports car in 2023, Porsche followed with the Taycan and announced further electrification plans, and Mercedes-Benz has expanded its EQ lineup with multiple models slated for release in the coming months. These launches have accelerated the shift toward electrification in the premium segment, creating a competitive environment where timing can be critical.

Industry observers note that the September entry positions the Torcal to benefit from the summer demand for new vehicles while avoiding the crowded holiday‑season launch window. However, the company must also contend with supply‑chain constraints and the need to secure battery supply for a 300‑mile range. Whether this timing will translate into a successful market entry remains to be seen, but the alignment with the broader electrification trend suggests the automaker has aimed to capitalize on current consumer interest and regulatory momentum.

title: Czinger 21C hybrid V8 with 3D‑printed components sets new lap records
content:
A new hybrid V8 powertrain has set a new lap record at the Circuit de la Sarthe, thanks to its unprecedented use of organic‑looking, 3‑D‑printed components. The engine, developed by the French automotive group Luminex Motors, blends a 3.0‑liter V8 with an electric motor that delivers a combined 700 horsepower. The hybrid system’s lightweight carbon‑fiber and polymer parts were printed using a high‑temperature resin that mimics the texture of natural tissue, allowing the engine to achieve a 30‑percent reduction in weight while maintaining structural integrity.

During the 2026 International Endurance Series, the Luminex prototype completed the 13.6‑kilometre circuit in 3:45.12, shaving 12 seconds off the previous record held by a conventional V8 race car. Engineers attribute the performance gain to the 3‑D‑printed components, which provide precise aerodynamic shaping and improved heat dissipation. The hybrid’s electric assist also delivers instant torque at low rpm, enabling faster acceleration out of the first corner.

Industry analysts see the breakthrough as a sign that additive manufacturing will become integral to high‑performance motorsport. By combining lightweight, bio‑inspired design with hybrid technology, Luminex Motors has demonstrated that 3‑D printing can deliver both speed and efficiency, potentially reshaping the engineering standards for future racing vehicles.
author: Ars Technica

title: Bentley previews first electric vehicle, the Torcal
content:
The company announced that its next‑generation model is scheduled for an official unveiling in late September, confirming speculation that has circulated among industry observers in recent weeks. The statement, released through a brief press release, indicated that the launch event will be held at the firm’s headquarters and will be streamed online for broader audience access. No additional details about the product’s specifications, pricing, or target market were disclosed at the time of the announcement.

Analysts expect the September rollout to align with the company’s annual product cycle and to potentially influence competitive dynamics within the sector. The forthcoming event is slated to include a live demonstration and a Q&A session with senior executives, offering stakeholders an opportunity to assess the model’s capabilities and strategic positioning. The company has indicated that further information will be made available in the weeks leading up to the unveiling.
author: Ars Technica

title: Even Realities Raises $150M, Reaches $1B Valuation
content:
Even Realities, a start‑up founded by former Apple engineers, announced that it has secured $150 million in new funding from Meituan and Tencent, valuing the company at $1 billion. The capital infusion follows a Series B round that underscores the growing interest in camera‑free augmented‑reality (AR) eyewear, a niche that promises enhanced privacy and lower power consumption compared to camera‑enabled counterparts.

The company’s flagship product is a lightweight pair of smart glasses that project digital information onto the wearer’s field of view without using any cameras. By relying on sensors such as inertial measurement units and depth cameras, Even Realities aims to deliver real‑time overlays for navigation, productivity, and entertainment while sidestepping the privacy concerns that have slowed broader AR adoption. The new investment will accelerate hardware development, expand the engineering team, and support market entry in key regions, including China and the United States.

With the backing of Meituan and Tencent, Even Realities is positioned to compete with larger AR players while carving out a distinct segment focused on privacy‑centric, low‑power eyewear. The company plans to begin pilot deployments with enterprise clients later this year, potentially setting the stage for a consumer launch in 2025.
author: TechCrunch

title: FCA urges stronger regulator powers to protect consumers from AI risks
content:
The Financial Conduct Authority’s landmark “Mills” review, which examines how artificial intelligence will reshape financial services from 2030 onward, warns that the rapid shift toward AI‑enabled offerings could magnify cyber‑crime and fraud risks for consumers. The assessment notes that firms are already moving from human‑led processes to automated, algorithm‑driven services for everyday banking, payments and investment advice, creating new vulnerabilities that existing regulatory frameworks may not fully address.

In response, the review urges ministers to strengthen the FCA’s powers, giving the regulator greater authority to intervene, enforce safeguards and oversee the deployment of AI across the sector. By enhancing oversight, the FCA aims to mitigate heightened threats while supporting responsible innovation, ensuring that the benefits of technology do not come at the expense of consumer protection.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Study finds AI drafting tools alter user messages on political topics, may affect public opinion
content:
Researchers from Oxford and the University of Potsdam have warned that minor alterations made by artificial‑intelligence tools when redrafting or summarising online content could trigger rapid, widespread shifts in public opinion. Their study finds that AI‑driven platforms, increasingly promoted by tech firms as efficient solutions for handling the daily surge of digital messages, are often embedding partisan slants into the text they process. The biases identified range from distinctly right‑wing to more liberal perspectives, affecting topics as sensitive as abortion, climate change and other political issues.

The analysis examined a broad sample of AI‑generated rewrites across multiple platforms, comparing the original messages with the altered outputs. Researchers observed that even subtle changes—such as word choice, framing or emphasis—can amplify particular viewpoints and diminish opposing arguments. Over time, these cumulative modifications may snowball, influencing how large audiences perceive and discuss contentious subjects, thereby reshaping long‑term public sentiment.

The findings highlight the need for greater transparency and oversight of AI content‑generation tools, especially as they become integral to information dissemination. Policymakers and technology providers are urged to consider safeguards that mitigate partisan distortion, ensuring that AI assistance does not inadvertently steer public discourse.
author: Guardian Technology

title: 19 dead, over 100 injured in Sri Lanka prison riot
content:
Police said that overnight clashes between inmates belonging to two rival drug gangs resulted in several injuries, prompting the transport of the wounded to Negombo Hospital, located north of the capital Colombo. The confrontation, which took place within a correctional facility, involved members of organized criminal groups and escalated into a violent exchange before authorities were able to intervene.

Medical teams at Negombo Hospital treated the injured, while prison officials and law‑enforcement agencies launched an investigation into the incident. Authorities indicated that the episode underscores ongoing security challenges within the prison system and pledged to review safety protocols to prevent similar occurrences in the future.
author: Euronews

title: England Defeats Mexico 3-2 to Reach World Cup Quarter-Finals
content:
England supporters erupted in celebration after the national team secured a dramatic 3‑2 victory over Mexico, a result that guarantees the Three Lions a place in the World Cup quarter‑finals. The win, achieved in a tightly contested match, saw England overturn a deficit to claim all three points and advance to the tournament’s knockout stage.

The victory, marked by a late surge that produced the decisive goals, not only propelled England into the quarter‑finals but also underscored the team's resilience in high‑pressure situations. As the squad prepares for its next opponent, the celebratory atmosphere among fans reflects both the significance of the triumph and the anticipation of the challenges that lie ahead in the competition.
author: Euronews

title: Hamas dissolves Gaza governing body, seeks technocratic committee
content:
Hamas has announced a significant change in its political strategy, a move that signals a new direction for the group that has governed the Gaza Strip since its 2007 takeover of the territory from rival Palestinian faction Fatah. The announcement came during a press briefing in Gaza City, where senior Hamas officials outlined a revised approach to governance and regional engagement.

The shift follows years of internal and external pressure on Hamas to broaden its political base and improve relations with other Palestinian factions and international actors. By redefining its policy priorities, Hamas aims to strengthen its administrative control, address humanitarian needs, and potentially open channels for dialogue with both the Palestinian Authority and external stakeholders.

The new strategy is expected to reshape Gaza’s political landscape, potentially altering the balance of power between Hamas and Fatah and influencing future negotiations over the region’s governance and security arrangements.
author: Euronews

title: Wildfire forces 500 evacuations in Castellon, Spain
content:
A wildfire ignited in the province of Castellón in eastern Spain on Tuesday, prompting the evacuation of roughly 500 residents from nearby villages. Local authorities declared a state of emergency as the blaze rapidly spread across the Valencia region, threatening homes, agricultural land and forested areas.

Firefighters on the ground, supported by aerial units deploying water‑dropping aircraft, have been working through the night to contain the flames. The emergency response, coordinated by the regional civil protection agency, includes the establishment of temporary shelters for evacuees and ongoing monitoring of weather conditions that could influence the fire’s behavior. As of the latest reports, the fire remains active, but containment efforts are progressing, and officials continue to assess the extent of damage and the need for further assistance.
author: Euronews

title: Hamas dissolves Gaza governing body, plans technocratic committee
content:
Hamas announced on Monday that it has dissolved its governing body in the Gaza Strip, ending nearly two decades of direct rule and establishing a technocratic committee to oversee the territory. The decision follows the group’s 2007 takeover of Gaza and its subsequent administration of the enclave’s civil and security affairs.

According to a statement released by the Hamas leadership, the new committee will be composed of experts in administration, finance, and public services, and will operate under the party’s broader political framework. The move is intended to streamline governance and address criticism over bureaucratic inefficiencies, while maintaining Hamas’s political control. The committee’s mandate will cover day‑to‑day management of public utilities, infrastructure, and social services, with oversight from senior Hamas officials.

This shift marks a significant change in Gaza’s political structure, potentially easing internal tensions and improving service delivery. Analysts note that the technocratic model could also be a response to external pressures and a strategy to present a more moderate image to international audiences. The new body will begin operations immediately, with its first appointments expected to be announced within the coming days.
author: France 24

title: Venezuelans volunteer to aid earthquake victims as death toll reaches 3,342
content:
Ten days after twin earthquakes struck Venezuela, the death toll remains uncertain, with official reports citing at least 3,342 fatalities. The most severely affected area is the northern coastal region, where the seismic shocks caused widespread devastation to infrastructure and homes. In the absence of a coordinated emergency response, survivors and volunteers from across the country have stepped in to provide medical care, secure temporary shelters, and conduct search operations for the missing.

On the ground, residents recount the chaos and the urgent need for assistance. Pascale Mariani and Maxime Pluvinet of France 24 spoke with locals who described makeshift triage tents set up in open spaces, community members sharing limited supplies, and the emotional toll of searching for loved ones amid collapsed buildings. The volunteers are working around the clock, coordinating with local authorities to prioritize the most vulnerable and to establish communication lines for those still trapped.

While the official figures may change as more information becomes available, the ongoing efforts by civilians underscore the critical gap in disaster relief. The situation remains fluid, with authorities and humanitarian groups continuing to assess damage and plan for long‑term recovery.
author: France 24

title: Millions Gather in Tehran for Supreme Leader Khamenei Funeral
content:
Vast crowds converged on Tehran on July 6 for the funeral procession of Iran’s slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, with authorities estimating that millions of people lined the streets. The final public tribute is scheduled to last approximately ten hours, during which mourners will witness the state‑sponsored ceremony and pay their respects to the former leader.  

The procession, which has drawn people from across the country, is part of a broader national mourning period that includes flags at half‑mast, moments of silence, and memorial services in major cities. Officials have arranged extensive security measures to manage the large crowds and to ensure the smooth flow of the event.  

Reza Sayah of France 24 has reported that the ceremony will feature traditional Islamic rites, speeches by senior clerics, and a display of the national flag. The event is expected to conclude with a final tribute at the mausoleum, marking the end of the public mourning period.
author: France 24

title: Europe rushes to buy Chinese air conditioners ahead of heatwave
content:
Hundreds of shoppers converged on supermarkets in Paris and its suburbs as a new heatwave approached, sparking scuffles and shouting as they vied for inexpensive air‑cooling units. The crowds, drawn by the promise of affordable relief, pushed past aisles and into checkout lines, turning otherwise routine grocery trips into chaotic scenes of competition.

The demand for cheap cooling has driven many Europeans toward Chinese-made air‑conditioners, a trend that has intensified despite ongoing trade tensions between Beijing and Brussels. Yena Lee of France 24 reports that the units are priced well below European standards, making them attractive to consumers seeking to beat the heat on a budget. However, the surge in purchases has raised questions about supply chain reliability and regulatory compliance.

Authorities have urged calm and warned that the rush could strain local supply chains and safety protocols. As the heatwave looms, officials are monitoring the situation to ensure that the scramble for cooling does not compromise public order or consumer safety.
author: France 24

title: England beat Mexico 3-2 as Norway eliminate Brazil 2-1 in World Cup 2026
content:
England’s “Three Lions” overcame the challenges of high altitude and a hostile home crowd to secure a 3‑2 victory over Mexico. Jude Bellingham, named man of the match, delivered a decisive burst of two goals within a two‑minute span, while Harry Kane’s successful penalty maintained England’s lead against a determined Mexican side. The win, achieved in the opening stages of the tournament, positions England firmly in contention as they advance to the next round.

In a parallel upset, five‑time champions Brazil were eliminated after a 2‑1 defeat to Norway, with Erling Haaland scoring both goals to clinch the win. Haaland’s performance underscored Norway’s resilience and ensured their progression, while Brazil’s early exit marks a significant shift in the competition’s landscape. Both results set the stage for a tightly contested knockout phase.
author: France 24

title: Hamas Dissolves Gaza Governing Body, Plans Technocratic Committee
content:
Hamas announced on July 7 that it would dissolve the governing body that has overseen the Gaza Strip for almost twenty years, paving the way for a technocratic committee to take charge of civilian governance. The move follows a long‑standing debate within the Palestinian leadership over how best to manage Gaza’s political and administrative affairs, and it signals a shift away from the factional structure that has dominated the region’s politics since the 2007 takeover.

The new committee, composed of experts and technocrats, is expected to oversee the day‑to‑day administration of Gaza and to lay the groundwork for a broader transition to civilian rule. However, questions remain about the committee’s composition, its mandate, and how it will navigate the complex political dynamics between Hamas, the Palestinian Authority, and external actors. Observers note that the decision could alter the balance of power within Gaza, but its success will depend on the committee’s ability to maintain stability while addressing the humanitarian and economic challenges that the Strip faces.

As the transition unfolds, international partners and local stakeholders will be watching closely to see whether the technocratic approach can deliver effective governance and restore confidence among Gaza’s residents. The outcome of this experiment could set a precedent for future governance reforms in the region.
author: France 24

title: Millions Attend Khamenei Funeral Procession in Tehran
content:
Tehran is hosting a massive funeral procession for Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, with millions of citizens lining the streets as the cortege moves through the capital. The ayatollah’s body has been on display for two days at the Grand Mosalla religious complex, allowing the public to pay their respects before the final rites.

Khamenei is scheduled to be interred in his hometown on July 10, concluding the state‑organized mourning period. Authorities have coordinated the burial logistics amid the large turnout, emphasizing the event’s significance for the nation’s political and religious leadership.
author: France 24

title: Millions attend funeral procession for Iran's late Supreme Leader
content:
Tehran’s main avenues were filled on Saturday with thousands of mourners taking part in a state‑organized procession honoring Iran’s late supreme leader. The tightly coordinated march, which began at the Imam Khomeini Square and wound through the city’s historic districts, featured flags, banners and speeches from senior clerics, underscoring the symbolic importance of the ceremony for the nation’s theocratic establishment.

Analysts view the large‑scale gathering as a deliberate display of domestic solidarity by the regime as it enters a new round of diplomatic talks with the United States aimed at easing long‑standing tensions. By staging a highly visible tribute, officials seek to project internal cohesion and political strength, reinforcing their negotiating position while signaling to both supporters and opponents that the leadership remains unified despite external pressures. The procession concluded without incident, and authorities have indicated that the forthcoming negotiations will proceed as scheduled.
author: DW World

title: Deadly clash at Sri Lankan prison kills inmates and guards
content:
A violent clash at a prison in Sri Lanka on Tuesday resulted in the deaths of several inmates and correctional staff, according to authorities. Police reports indicate that the confrontation, which erupted in the early afternoon, left at least eight people dead and more than a dozen injured. The incident occurred at the Jaffna Central Prison, a facility that has faced criticism for overcrowding and limited security resources in recent years.

Investigators say the violence began when a group of inmates allegedly attempted to seize weapons from the guard’s station, triggering a firefight that quickly spread across multiple cell blocks. The Sri Lanka Prison Service confirmed that the deceased include four inmates and four guards, while hospital officials confirmed that three of the injured inmates and four of the staff are in critical condition. The Ministry of Justice has pledged a full inquiry into the circumstances that led to the outbreak, and the government has announced plans to review security protocols at all correctional facilities.

The incident has drawn attention to the broader issue of prison conditions in Sri Lanka, where overcrowding and insufficient staffing have been long‑standing concerns. The government has stated that it will cooperate with independent bodies to assess the situation and implement reforms aimed at preventing future incidents. The investigation is ongoing, with authorities expected to release further details once the forensic and administrative review is complete.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Massive crowds attend funeral procession for Iran's Supreme Leader Khamenei
content:
Enormous crowds have assembled in Tehran for a third consecutive day to mourn the death of Iranian President‑elect Mahdi Al‑Khalaji, who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in Syria on Monday. The crowds, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, have turned the capital’s main avenues into impromptu memorials, with mourners carrying flags, candles and banners that read “Revenge for the martyrs.”  

Security forces have tightened control over the demonstrations, deploying police and military units to secure key intersections and to prevent clashes with protestors. The gatherings have been accompanied by a wave of anti‑U.S. and anti‑Israeli rhetoric, with speakers and social media posts calling for retaliation against both nations. Despite the calls for vengeance, authorities have urged participants to remain peaceful, warning that any escalation could lead to a crackdown.  

The sustained mourning and calls for retribution underscore the heightened tensions between Iran and the United States, as well as the broader regional fallout from the strike. While the Iranian government has condemned the attack as a violation of international law, it has also signaled that it will not seek to engage in direct military conflict. The situation remains fluid as Tehran’s security apparatus continues to monitor the crowds and the potential for further unrest.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Heatwave Exposes Inequalities in France
content:
Heatwaves have intensified across the country, and residents in low‑income neighborhoods are bearing the brunt of the rising temperatures.  With limited access to air conditioning, cooling centers, or affordable housing, many families are forced to stay in poorly ventilated homes as the mercury climbs above 35 °C (95 °F).  The situation has prompted a wave of criticism from analysts who argue that the government’s current heat‑action plan falls short of protecting the most vulnerable.

Experts point to several gaps in the response.  While the administration has announced temporary cooling stations and a modest subsidy program for electricity bills, the rollout has been uneven and funding insufficient.  Analysts also note that the plan lacks a comprehensive strategy for long‑term adaptation, such as retrofitting public buildings with better insulation or expanding green spaces in high‑density districts.  They warn that without a more robust, equitable approach, the heatwave could exacerbate existing health disparities and strain municipal resources.

In light of these concerns, policymakers are under pressure to accelerate and broaden their efforts.  The government has pledged to review the heat‑action framework and increase investment in community cooling infrastructure.  As the season progresses, stakeholders will be watching closely to see whether the revised measures can effectively mitigate the impact of extreme heat on low‑income populations.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Heat intensifies hardship in Gaza displacement camps
content:
Scorching heat has intensified the humanitarian crisis in Gaza’s displacement camps, where residents already face overcrowding, limited water supplies and inadequate shelter. According to satellite data, temperatures in the region have risen to over 40 °C (104 °F) for several consecutive days, a level that has pushed many families to seek relief in makeshift shade and open water sources that are often contaminated. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that more than 1.2 million people are living in temporary camps across the Gaza Strip, with many lacking access to electricity, clean water, and proper sanitation facilities.

Health agencies on the ground warn that the extreme heat is exacerbating dehydration, heat exhaustion, and respiratory illnesses, particularly among children and the elderly. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has increased the distribution of water purification tablets and portable cooling devices, while Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has set up temporary medical posts to treat heat‑related conditions. Despite these efforts, the camps remain vulnerable to further deterioration as the summer season continues, underscoring the urgent need for sustained humanitarian assistance and infrastructure improvements to protect the displaced population.
author: Al Jazeera

title: FIFA suspends Balogun after Trump‑related comment, draws criticism
content:
FIFA announced an unprecedented decision on Thursday that has ignited a widespread furore across the global football community. The governing body’s move, described by officials as a historic step forward for the sport, was revealed during a press conference in Zurich and immediately prompted intense debate among national associations, clubs, players’ unions and fans.

Critics have condemned the decision as disruptive, citing concerns over competitive balance, scheduling and the potential impact on existing tournament structures. Several football federations have lodged formal objections, while prominent players’ representatives have called for further consultation before implementation. FIFA has indicated that it will convene an emergency summit of stakeholders to address the controversy and outline a timeline for any possible adjustments, signaling an effort to mitigate the backlash while maintaining its strategic objectives.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump lobbying and FIFA reversal spark controversy before USA vs Belgium World Cup last‑16 match
content:
President Donald Trump’s personal lobbying of FIFA officials this week has sparked a fresh wave of controversy ahead of the upcoming knockout round of the international tournament. According to sources familiar with the discussions, the U.S. president urged the governing body to alter the match schedule and venue to accommodate a high‑profile American sponsor, arguing that the change would boost viewership and revenue. In response, FIFA announced a last‑minute reversal of its earlier decision, moving the fixture to a larger stadium in a neighboring country and adjusting kickoff times to align with prime‑time U.S. television slots.

The abrupt shift has drawn criticism from several national teams, players’ unions and fan groups, who contend that the alteration undermines the competition’s integrity and favors commercial interests over sporting fairness. FIFA’s executive committee defended the move as a “strategic adjustment” intended to maximize global exposure, while acknowledging the timing of the decision was influenced by recent diplomatic outreach. As the knockout match approaches, organizers are working to finalize logistics, and observers note that the episode may set a precedent for future political involvement in the sport’s scheduling decisions.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill at least six and wound over 20
content:
Israeli airstrikes targeted residential areas in Gaza City and the southern city of Khan Younis on Thursday, leaving more than 20 individuals injured, according to medical officials monitoring the conflict. The casualties, reported by doctors working in field hospitals and clinics, include both civilians and members of local security forces, and the wounded are being treated for a range of injuries from shrapnel wounds to burns.

The strikes come amid an intensified phase of the Israel‑Hamas war that began in early October, during which both sides have exchanged heavy fire and civilian infrastructure has been repeatedly hit. Health authorities in the enclave have warned that the growing number of injured strains already limited medical resources, while international agencies continue to call for the protection of civilians and unhindered access to humanitarian aid.
author: Al Jazeera

title: UN warns of potential catastrophe as RSF besieges El-Obeid
content:
The United Nations has issued an urgent warning that the city of el‑Obeid in Sudan faces the risk of a humanitarian catastrophe following a wave of atrocities committed by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in the neighboring town of el‑Fasher last year. The warning was released by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) after field assessments indicated a sharp increase in civilian casualties, forced displacement, and the destruction of essential infrastructure in the region.

UN officials say that the aftermath of the RSF attacks in el‑Fasher has left thousands of residents without access to food, clean water, and medical services, creating a precarious situation that could spill over into el‑Obeid, a major population centre in North Kordofan. Humanitarian agencies are calling for immediate protection measures, the safe passage of aid convoys, and the establishment of humanitarian corridors to prevent a broader crisis. The UN has appealed to all parties in the Sudan conflict to respect international humanitarian law and to allow unimpeded delivery of assistance to the affected communities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Thousands gather in Tehran for Khamenei funeral procession
content:
A crowd gathered in the city’s central square on Saturday, brandishing Iranian national flags alongside red banners that read “Vengeance for the former Supreme Leader’s war death.” Organizers said the demonstration was intended to honor the memory of the late leader, whom they claim died as a result of foreign aggression during the Iran‑Iraq conflict, and to call for accountability for those they hold responsible.

The procession moved through main thoroughfares, with participants chanting slogans and displaying the symbols of mourning and retribution. Local authorities monitored the event, noting that the gathering remained peaceful despite the emotionally charged messages. The rally underscores ongoing sentiments among segments of the population who continue to invoke the former leader’s legacy in contemporary political discourse.
author: BBC World

title: Hamilton Frustrated with Ferrari Strategy at British Grand Prix
content:
Lewis Hamilton expressed frustration following the British Grand Prix, citing a late strategic decision by his Ferrari team that he believes cost him a chance to secure second place. The seven-time world champion, who finished third behind teammate Charles Leclerc and Mercedes’ George Russell, revealed that Ferrari’s call to pit him under a late safety car period disrupted his race trajectory. Hamilton, who had been in second position at the time, lost track position to Russell, who opted to remain on the track, leaving him unable to reclaim the spot before the race concluded under the safety car.  

The race unfolded with Leclerc clinching victory, while Hamilton’s afternoon was described as “nothing going right” due to a combination of tactical missteps and competitive pressures. Ferrari’s decision to pit Hamilton for fresh tires during the safety car phase, intended to optimize race strategy, instead allowed Russell to maintain his advantage. Hamilton’s criticism underscores the high-stakes nature of Formula 1 race strategies, where split-second choices can dramatically alter outcomes. With the season entering a critical phase, the incident highlights the ongoing challenges Hamilton faces in balancing team dynamics and individual performance.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Arthur Fery Advances to Wimbledon Fourth Round
content:
Arthur Fery, a wildcard entrant, will make his grand slam second-week debut at Wimbledon on Monday when he faces former world No. 3 Grigor Dimitrov in the fourth round. The 24-year-old British player, now the last remaining home hope in the men’s singles draw, has stunned the tennis world with a three-match winning streak that propelled him to this stage. Fery, who had never advanced beyond the second round of a major tournament before this year, has embraced the spotlight with composure, stating he will ignore social media distractions and focus solely on the challenge ahead.  

Fery’s journey to the fourth round marks a career milestone, as he transitions from relative obscurity to center stage at Wimbledon. The British number two, ranked 147th in the ATP, has navigated a path of unseeded opponents with tactical discipline, showcasing resilience and adaptability. His run has drawn attention for its unexpected nature, with analysts noting his ability to thrive under pressure. Against Dimitrov, a former top-10 player with a 2022 Wimbledon quarterfinal pedigree, Fery faces a sterner test but remains undeterred, emphasizing his readiness to compete at the highest level.  

As the sole British representative in the men’s singles second week, Fery’s performance carries added significance for UK tennis. His match against Dimitrov will be a litmus test for his ability to sustain momentum against elite opposition. While Dimitrov’s experience and serve-volley style pose challenges, Fery’s underdog status and recent form suggest a compelling contest. The outcome will not only shape his own trajectory but also highlight the unpredictable nature of Wimbledon, where determination and opportunity often collide.

title: NCAA president backs Protect College Sports Act, warns against walking away
content:
The Protect College Sports Act has drawn praise from the NCAA, with President Charlie Baker stating that the bill “effectively deals with many of the issues facing our industry.” Baker emphasized that the legislation aims to create a national framework that would standardize rules for national championships and competitions, ensuring a level playing field for all participating schools. He noted that the Act addresses longstanding concerns about player compensation, eligibility, and the governance of collegiate athletics.

The bill, which has garnered bipartisan support, seeks to clarify the rights of student‑athletes while preserving the amateur status that underpins college sports. By establishing uniform guidelines, the NCAA hopes to reduce legal disputes and streamline compliance for institutions across the country. The Act also includes provisions for enhanced transparency in recruiting and financial aid practices, aligning with broader efforts to modernize the regulatory environment for collegiate athletics.

If enacted, the Protect College Sports Act could reshape the landscape of college sports by providing clearer standards and reducing the need for state‑by‑state regulation. The NCAA’s endorsement signals a potential shift toward a more cohesive national system, which stakeholders anticipate will benefit both athletes and universities by fostering consistency and fairness in competition.

title: Trump Heads to Ankara to Enforce NATO Defense Spending Promises
content:
President Donald Trump is traveling to Ankara, Turkey, to attend the annual NATO summit. His presence follows a campaign last year in which he urged member states to increase their defense spending, a pledge that has become a central focus of the current meeting.

At this year’s gathering, Trump aims to press NATO allies to honor those commitments, highlighting the importance of collective security and the need for sustained investment in military capabilities. The summit will also address broader strategic issues, including deterrence against regional threats and the coordination of defense budgets across the alliance.

The outcome of the discussions will shape NATO’s future financial and operational priorities. While the conference is expected to reinforce the alliance’s cohesion, the extent to which member nations will meet the targeted spending levels remains to be seen.
author: NPR Politics

title: Louisville Voters Received Wrong Ballots for Years
content:
In Louisville, Kentucky, a recent investigation by Louisville Public Media has uncovered that a number of voters have been cast on incorrect ballots for several election cycles. The investigation traced the issue to a series of administrative errors in the voter registration database, which caused mismatches between voter records and the ballots distributed at polling places. As a result, some ballots were printed with the wrong candidate lists, leading to votes that did not reflect the intended choices of those voters.

The findings highlight the importance of accurate voter data management. Officials from the Jefferson County Election Board confirmed that corrective measures are underway, including a review of registration records and a plan to reissue ballots where discrepancies were identified. They also announced that additional training will be provided to election staff to prevent similar errors in future elections. While the investigation did not find evidence of intentional fraud, it underscores the need for robust checks to ensure the integrity of the voting process.
author: NPR Politics

title: Former Marine argues veteran candidates can boost bipartisan cooperation
content:
Former Marine and author Lt. Col. Daniel R. Hayes has released a new book arguing that veterans who run for public office can infuse Washington with the courage needed to work across party lines. In the 240‑page volume, *Brave the Divide*, Hayes contends that the discipline, teamwork, and mission‑first mindset cultivated in the armed forces translate into a bipartisan approach to governance. He cites his own experience in the Marine Corps and in the political arena to illustrate how veterans can bridge ideological gaps.

Hayes outlines several mechanisms by which veterans may foster cross‑party collaboration. He points to the shared sense of duty and the emphasis on mission over ideology that veterans bring to the table, suggesting that these qualities can help lawmakers prioritize national interests over partisan gains. The book also surveys recent congressional races in which veteran candidates have won seats in both major parties, noting that their campaigns often emphasize unity and pragmatic solutions rather than partisan rhetoric. Hayes argues that this trend could help restore public confidence in a legislative body that has been mired in gridlock.

The release of *Brave the Divide* comes as the United States approaches a midterm election cycle marked by intense polarization. Hayes’ message—veterans can be a unifying force in Washington—offers a potential blueprint for reducing partisan friction. Whether his call for a bipartisan veteran presence will translate into tangible legislative change remains to be seen, but the book has already sparked discussion among political analysts and veteran advocacy groups about the role of military experience in shaping future policy debates.

title: US Parties Mark Independence Day
content:
On July 4th, the United States saw a flurry of political activity as the two major parties seized the holiday to present their visions for the nation’s future. Republican leaders highlighted a platform centered on economic growth, deregulation, and a strengthened national defense, citing the need to protect American jobs and maintain global leadership. Democratic figures, meanwhile, focused on expanding healthcare access, addressing climate change, and investing in infrastructure, framing their agenda as a path to long‑term prosperity and equity.

Both parties staged events across the country, from televised rallies in Washington, D.C., to local gatherings in key swing states. Speakers emphasized the holiday’s themes of freedom and unity, using patriotic imagery to underscore their policy proposals. The Republican message stressed individual responsibility and fiscal conservatism, while the Democratic narrative underscored collective action and social investment, reflecting the ideological divide that has defined recent political discourse.

As the holiday concluded, observers noted that the speeches reinforced each party’s core messages ahead of the upcoming mid‑term elections. The contrasting visions presented on July 4th are expected to shape campaign strategies and voter expectations in the months to come, highlighting the enduring role of national holidays as platforms for political communication.

title: Cancer Screening Disparities Found Across SOGI Groups
content:
A recent study published in the journal *Cancer* has highlighted enduring gaps in preventive cancer care among people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities (SOGI). The research, which analyzed national screening data, found that rates of cervical and breast cancer screening are consistently lower in LGBTQ+ populations compared with their heterosexual and cisgender peers.

The investigators examined screening uptake across a range of SOGI groups, noting that transgender and non‑binary individuals, as well as gay and bisexual men, were disproportionately under‑screened. The authors attribute these disparities to a combination of factors, including provider bias, lack of culturally competent care, and systemic barriers that limit access to routine health services. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions to improve screening rates and reduce late‑stage cancer diagnoses in these communities.

The study’s authors call for enhanced provider education, inclusive health policies, and community outreach to address the identified gaps. By ensuring equitable access to cervical and breast cancer screening, health systems can work toward reducing the higher cancer burden that disproportionately affects SOGI populations.

title: ITV Sells Media Arm to Sky
content:
The BBC and ITV have announced a joint venture to launch a new streaming platform aimed at challenging the dominance of global players such as Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon Prime Video. The partnership, which will combine the broadcasters’ extensive libraries of drama, comedy and factual programming, is intended to provide a distinctly British alternative that can compete on both content quality and pricing.

Under the agreement, the two companies will pool their content catalogues and share the costs of original production, marketing and technology infrastructure. The platform will be available on multiple devices, with a subscription model that includes a free tier supported by advertising and a premium tier offering ad‑free viewing. Industry analysts note that the combined reach of the BBC’s public‑service remit and ITV’s commercial audience gives the new service a unique positioning in the UK market, potentially attracting viewers who prefer domestic content over international offerings.

If the launch succeeds, the BBC‑ITV platform could force a shift in the streaming landscape, compelling rivals to rethink their strategies for the UK audience. The broadcasters have said they will monitor subscriber growth closely and adjust their content mix accordingly, signalling a long‑term commitment to competing with the likes of Netflix and Disney+.

title: Southern Europe Wildfires Force Thousands to Evacuate
content:
Wildfires swept across Southern Europe on Monday, forcing thousands of residents to leave their homes and prompting authorities to take drastic safety measures. The flames, which spread through parts of Spain, Portugal and France, were part of a larger wave of high‑temperature, low‑humidity conditions that have plagued the region for weeks.

In response to the escalating threat, officials in the affected areas ordered the evacuation of entire communities and imposed a ban on spectators at a scheduled stage of the Tour de France. The race, which traditionally attracts large crowds, was held in a region where the fire risk was deemed too high for public attendance. Organizers confirmed that the stage would proceed with a reduced audience, and emergency services remained on standby to assist evacuees and support firefighting efforts.

The situation remains fluid as teams and local authorities monitor the fire’s progression. While the Tour de France will continue under tighter security protocols, the priority for emergency responders remains the safe evacuation of civilians and containment of the blazes that threaten both lives and the region’s infrastructure.
author: Phys.org

title: China’s Tianwen-2 probe reaches asteroid after 1‑billion km journey
content:
China’s Tianwen‑2 asteroid‑sampling probe reached its target on Monday, the China National Space Administration (CNSA) announced. The spacecraft, launched in 2021, has traveled roughly 1 billion kilometres (620 million miles) over a period of more than a year to arrive at the near‑Earth asteroid 2019 R1.

Tianwen‑2 is designed to collect surface material from the asteroid and return it to Earth for scientific analysis. The probe’s journey included a complex trajectory that involved multiple gravity‑assist manoeuvres and precise navigation to rendezvous with the small body. The mission is part of China’s broader effort to demonstrate advanced planetary‑sample‑return capabilities and to expand knowledge of asteroid composition.

The successful arrival marks a milestone for the Chinese space programme and provides a new opportunity to study the primordial material that makes up the solar system’s building blocks. The collected samples are expected to be analysed by Chinese laboratories in the coming months, potentially offering fresh insights into the origins of planetary bodies.

title: Category 5 Super Typhoon Hits U.S. Pacific Islands, Rota Reports Major Damage
content:
A super‑typhoon with winds equivalent to a Category 5 hurricane swept across the U.S. Pacific territories of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam on Monday, prompting emergency officials to issue warnings and mobilize response teams. The storm, classified as a “super typhoon” by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, made landfall with sustained winds exceeding 150 mph, bringing torrential rain and widespread flooding to the region.

Authorities reported “major” damage on the small island of Rota, noting destroyed homes, downed power lines, and blocked roadways, while neighboring islands also experienced significant infrastructure impacts. Federal and local agencies have begun damage assessments and are coordinating relief efforts, with additional resources slated to arrive in the coming days to support recovery and restore essential services.

title: TV Game Show Probability Puzzle Explained
content:
A new probability puzzle has been introduced on a popular television game show, challenging contestants and viewers alike with a scenario that blends chance and strategy. The show's compere announced that, at the conclusion of each episode, two participants will be selected at random and escorted to separate booths, isolated from one another. The puzzle’s premise hinges on the unknown variables governing the selection process and the subsequent conditions inside the booths, prompting audiences to calculate the likelihood of various outcomes based on limited information.

The puzzle quickly gained attention for its elegant simplicity and the mathematical reasoning it demands, encouraging both amateur enthusiasts and seasoned statisticians to engage with the problem. As the show progresses, viewers are invited to submit their solutions, fostering an interactive community around the challenge. Organizers have indicated that the puzzle will become a recurring feature, aiming to promote analytical thinking and public interest in probability theory.

title: Waning Crescent Moon Passes Over Pleiades on 11 July
content:
On the night of 11 July, the waning crescent moon will glide past the Pleiades star cluster (M45, the Seven Sisters) in the early hours, just before dawn. From London, a view east‑north‑east at 3 a.m. BST will show the moon moving along the same line of sight as the bright cluster. Astronomers note that the sky will begin to brighten as the day approaches, making a clear, low horizon essential for observers to spot the pairing of moon and cluster.

The Pleiades, a popular target for amateur astronomers, will appear as a tight grouping of stars that can be seen with the naked eye. The moon’s passage offers a brief moment when the crescent can be seen close to the cluster, creating a striking visual effect for those with binoculars or a telescope. Observers are advised to check local weather conditions and light‑pollution levels to maximize visibility of this celestial event.

content:
Tom Tunguz’s recent analysis, published on his blog, projects that cumulative spending on artificial‑intelligence technologies will reach a financial breakeven point by 2029. The forecast is based on current growth rates in AI research and development, escalating cloud‑compute costs, and the expanding market for AI‑driven products and services. Tunguz argues that while early‑stage investments have driven rapid adoption, the sector’s revenue streams—particularly from enterprise software, generative‑AI tools, and automation platforms—are expected to scale sufficiently to offset the high capital outlays within the next decade.

title: Agility Robotics to go public via SPAC, CEO says home robot not imminent
content:
Agility Robotics, the Boston‑based maker of the bipedal robot Cassie, has announced a merger with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) as its next step toward going public. The move follows a wave of high‑profile valuations in the humanoid robotics sector, where firms such as Boston Dynamics and other emerging startups have sought to secure large sums through venture funding and IPO hype. By contrast, Agility Robotics has emphasized incremental progress on its hardware and software platforms, positioning the SPAC deal as a means to secure capital while maintaining a disciplined focus on product execution.

The SPAC, led by investment firm XYZ Capital, will provide Agility Robotics with an estimated $200 million in equity capital and a $1.2 billion valuation, according to the merger agreement filed with the SEC. The partnership is intended to accelerate development of the company’s next‑generation robots, which are designed for warehouse automation, logistics, and industrial inspection. Executives have indicated that the infusion of funds will support scaling of production, expansion of the engineering team, and the rollout of pilot deployments with key commercial partners.

With the SPAC merger set to close in the coming months, Agility Robotics aims to demonstrate that a steady, execution‑driven growth model can compete in a market that often rewards speculative valuations. The company’s strategy underscores a broader industry trend toward pragmatic, revenue‑focused development, as robotics firms seek to translate prototype success into sustainable commercial operations.
author: TechCrunch

title: Elbit reports Israeli system tracked 850,000 targets in Gaza and Lebanon wars
content:
Israel’s largest defence contractor, Elbit Systems, disclosed at a military conference in London that its Tzayad digital army programme has been used to map people, vehicles and other objects in real time across the country’s active war zones. The system, integrated into Israel’s command and control network, identified roughly 1,000 potential targets each day during the first two years of the conflicts in Gaza and Lebanon, according to a presentation by the company.

Between 7 October 2023 and the end of 2025, the Tzayad platform recorded a total of 850,000 targets in real time across all Israeli theatres of war. Elbit Systems highlighted the programme’s role in providing continuous situational awareness for military operations, emphasizing its contribution to the rapid detection and assessment of threats. The figures illustrate the scale of data processing undertaken by Israel’s digital battlefield infrastructure during the ongoing hostilities.
author: Guardian Technology

title: China targets dexterous robotic hands to advance embodied AI
content:
The push to create “embodied AI” is now centered on developing dexterous robotic hands capable of matching the flexibility and precision of human fingers. Human hands, with their dense network of nerves and intricate musculature, can perform tasks such as tying shoelaces or buttoning shirts without conscious effort—a level of coordinated control that has eluded machines for millennia. Recent advances in artificial‑intelligence algorithms, tactile sensing, and lightweight actuation are allowing a handful of firms, especially in China, to integrate real‑time perception with fine‑motor control, moving humanoid robots beyond novelty demonstrations toward practical applications in manufacturing, logistics, and personal assistance.

Chinese companies including Alibaba’s DAMO Academy, Horizon Robotics, and UBTech are investing heavily in research that combines deep reinforcement learning with high‑resolution force feedback to teach robots how to grasp, manipulate, and adapt to varied objects. Parallel efforts in the United States and Europe are exploring similar approaches, but the concentration of funding and talent in China has accelerated prototype development, with several labs reporting successful trials of multi‑fingered hands that can perform tasks such as assembling small components or handling delicate items. If these technologies mature, they could transform humanoid robots from laboratory curiosities into viable tools for industry and everyday life, marking a significant milestone in the broader AI and robotics landscape.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Scottish AI datacentre project unlikely to meet renewable power promises
content:
A Guardian investigation has revealed that the £8.2 billion artificial‑intelligence datacentre slated for Lanarkshire, Scotland, has been promoted on the basis of misleading claims about its power supply. When the project was announced in January, the UK government and the developers – US‑based CoreWeave and Scottish firm DataVita – asserted that the complex would be powered entirely by on‑site renewable energy and would be operational by 2030. Internal communications obtained by the newspaper, however, show that both parties privately acknowledged a “power provision issue” and that the plan to deliver a nuclear‑reactor‑level electricity output to the rural site was not realistic. The discrepancy has raised questions about the feasibility of the broader “AI growth zones” policy, which aims to attract high‑tech investment to designated regions across Britain.

The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the project’s promised economic benefits, including job creation and regional prosperity. Critics argue that the reliance on uncertain energy infrastructure undermines the viability of the datacentre and could set a precedent for other AI initiatives that are marketed without solid technical foundations. As the government and developers face mounting pressure to clarify the power strategy, the Lanarkshire site stands as a test case for the credibility of the nation’s AI development agenda.

title: Morning news bulletin released on July 6, 2026
content:
On July 6, 2026, Europe’s headlines were shaped by a mix of climate policy, geopolitical shifts, and cultural milestones. The European Union convened an emergency summit in Brussels to finalize a new carbon‑pricing framework that raises the EU Emissions Trading System cap by 15 % for 2027, a move aimed at meeting the 2035 net‑zero target. At the same time, the United Kingdom announced a revised free‑trade agreement with the EU, easing customs checks on agricultural goods while tightening data‑protection standards.

In the broader geopolitical arena, the ceasefire brokered between Russia and Ukraine took effect after a week of negotiations in Geneva, with both sides agreeing to a phased withdrawal of heavy artillery from contested zones. Meanwhile, a coordinated cyber‑attack on several EU power‑grid operators prompted the European Cybersecurity Agency to issue an urgent alert, citing a new strain of malware that exploited outdated SCADA protocols. In the world of business, the merger of Germany’s Deutsche Bank and France’s Société Générale was approved, creating the continent’s largest banking group by assets and signaling a shift toward greater consolidation in the European financial sector.

Culturally, the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest concluded in Milan, where Italy’s representative won with a record‑breaking score, sparking celebrations across the continent. The Venice Biennale opened its latest exhibition, “Future Landscapes,” featuring works that explore climate change through digital media. Travel advisories were updated by the EU, warning of a newly identified respiratory virus variant that could affect seasonal tourism in the Mediterranean. Together, these stories underscore a Europe that is grappling with environmental imperatives, security challenges, and a vibrant cultural scene as it moves toward the second half of the decade.
author: Euronews

title: Activists use red paint to protest Pamplona bullfighting
content:
Animal‑rights activists staged a visual protest in Pamplona on Monday, covering themselves in red paint to symbolize blood before the start of the San Fermin Festival. The demonstration took place near the city’s historic bullring, where the opening bullfight is traditionally held, and was intended to draw attention to the activists’ demand for an end to the centuries‑old bullfighting practice.

Organizers of the protest, representing several animal‑welfare groups, positioned themselves in the crowd as the festival’s opening ceremony began, chanting slogans and distributing flyers that called for legislative bans on bullfighting. Local police monitored the event, reported no arrests, and allowed the demonstration to proceed without disrupting the scheduled performances. The San Fermin organizers reiterated their commitment to preserving the cultural heritage of the festival, while city officials noted that the protest reflects a growing public debate over the future of bullfighting in Spain.
author: Euronews

title: Iran holds funeral for late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei as coffin passes through Tehran
content:
Thousands of mourners gathered in Tehran on Saturday as Iran commenced funeral ceremonies for the late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who died at the age of 86. Khamenei, who had held the nation’s highest religious and political office since 1989, was laid to rest in the Imam Reza shrine complex, a site traditionally reserved for the most senior clerics. The state‑organized proceedings featured a procession through the capital’s main avenues, with flags at half‑mast and a period of national mourning declared by the government.

The ceremonies were attended by senior officials, members of the Revolutionary Guard, and representatives of allied political factions, underscoring Khamenei’s central role in shaping Iran’s domestic and foreign policies. Security forces were deployed to manage the large crowds, while televised broadcasts relayed the rites to a broader audience. The funeral marks a pivotal moment for Iran’s leadership structure, as the Assembly of Experts prepares to select a successor to the position that has defined the country’s direction for more than three decades.
author: Euronews

title: Australia and Fiji Sign Mutual Defence Pact Amid China Missile Test
content:
On Thursday, Australia signed a new defence treaty with the United States and the Philippines, formalising a trilateral security framework that will expand joint training, intelligence sharing and rapid response cooperation across the Indo‑Pacific. The agreement, which builds on earlier bilateral pacts, is intended to enhance collective deterrence against potential threats in a region that has seen growing military activity.

The treaty’s signing coincided with a report from Chinese state media that a Chinese submarine had test‑launched a long‑range ballistic missile in the South Pacific. The launch, described by Xinhua as a “routine exercise,” prompted Australia to issue a sharp rebuke, calling the action a destabilising threat to regional security. The incident underscores the heightened tensions that accompany the new security arrangement.

Together, the treaty and the Chinese missile test illustrate the complex security environment of the Indo‑Pacific. Australia’s move to deepen ties with the United States and the Philippines signals its commitment to maintaining stability, while the Chinese launch highlights the continuing challenges of ensuring peace and predictability in the region.

title: England defeats Mexico 3-2 in World Cup last-16
content:
England advanced to the quarter‑finals of the World Cup after a 3‑2 victory over Mexico in the last‑16 round, eliminating the host nation’s campaign. The match, played in Qatar, saw England secure a late winner, prompting a surge of celebration among English supporters while simultaneously delivering a decisive blow to Mexico’s hopes of progressing further.

In Mexico City, crowds gathered at public squares and sports bars to watch the game live, their reactions oscillating between jubilation and disappointment as the scoreline shifted. When England scored the decisive goal, many fans expressed heartbreak, yet some also applauded the competitive spirit of the encounter. The loss concludes Mexico’s tournament run, leaving the nation to reflect on its performance as it looks ahead to future international competitions.

title: Norway defeats Brazil 2-1 in World Cup round of 16, Haaland scores twice
content:
Norway advanced to the quarter‑finals of the World Cup after a 2–1 victory over Brazil in the round of 16. The match, played on Tuesday in Doha, saw the Scandinavian side overturn a 0–1 deficit with two late goals from striker Erling Haaland, who struck in the 79th and 90th minutes.

Haaland’s brace lifted Norway to a 2–1 win and brought his tournament tally to seven goals, placing him level with Argentina’s Lionel Messi and France’s Kylian Mbappé at the top of the competition’s scoring chart. Brazil’s elimination ends their campaign earlier than expected, while Norway’s triumph marks a historic progression in the tournament.

title: Iran holds funeral procession for late Supreme Leader Khamenei in Tehran
content:
The funeral procession for Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei departed Monday morning from Tehran, as reported by state television. The march, part of a state‑sponsored funeral that has spanned three days, was broadcast across the capital’s streets, underscoring the regime’s intent to project unity and strength amid the national mourning.

The ceremony has been staged as a display of solidarity, with security forces and religious officials lining the route and flanking the coffin. The third day of the funeral has been marked by large crowds, flag‑bearing contingents, and coordinated speeches from senior clerics, all aimed at reinforcing the government’s narrative of resilience and cohesion in the wake of the leader’s passing.

As the state funeral continues, Iranian authorities are maintaining a tight schedule of commemorations, with further ceremonies planned for the following days. The procession’s televised coverage is part of a broader effort to consolidate public sentiment and signal the continuity of the current political order.
